extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on patentable subject-matter and anticipation (novelty) under the Patent Act for use in examination and prosecution of Canadian patent applications. Covers definitions of statutory categories, excluded subject-matter, and detailed tests for anticipation and prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine (statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A “machine” is the mechanical and/or physical embodiment of any function or mode of operation designed to accomplish a particular effect, wherein the parts of the machine cooperate to accomplish the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A machine can be considered to be “any device that transmits a force or directs its application”, or “a device that enables energy from one source to be modified and transmitted as energy in a different form or for a different purpose”. A machine may be claimed as a device, as an apparatus, or a system, for example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture (statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A “manufacture” has been broadly defined as “a non-living mechanistic product or process” and as being the process of making technical articles or material by the application of physical labour or mechanical power; or the article or material made by such a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes making by hand, by machine, industrially, or by mass production; refers to technical articles or material made by such processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter (statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A “composition of matter” refers to physical and/or chemical substances, compounds and compositions, and includes combinations of ingredients, whether combined as a chemical union or physical mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term implies ingredients must be perceptible in space and have mechanical mass. Scope must be limited so as not to render other categories redundant (see Harvard College v. Canada).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions must have a practicable (non-disembodied) form
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is a solution to a practical problem and must be something with physical existence, or something that manifests a discernible effect or change (a 'practical form' or 'practicable form').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disembodied idea, concept or discovery is not patentable unless incorporated in a practical form. A disembodied idea is not per se patentable but may be if it has a method of practical application (Shell Oil Co. v. Commissioner of Patents). The idea that leads to an invention is not the invention; invention involves the act that results in a new product, result, process or combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific principles and abstract theorems (excluded subject-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 27(8) of the Patent Act: 'No patent shall be granted for any mere scientific principle or abstract theorem.' This excludes mathematical formulae, natural phenomena and laws of nature when claimed in a general sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusions apply when the subject-matter is claimed in a general/abstract sense, but not when a scientific principle, law of nature or mathematical formula is relied upon in operating a practical form of an invention. Claims directed to scientific principles/abstract theorems will be identified as defective under subsection 27(8) and section 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of medical treatment or surgery (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method or process of surgery or therapy on living humans or animals is not considered to be within the scope of the meaning of invention as set out in section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See section 23.03 for detailed consideration; such methods are treated as non-statutory subject-matter for patenting purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher life forms (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher life forms are excluded from patentability by virtue of their not being either manufactures or compositions of matter within the definition of invention in section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See section 23.02.01 for detailed consideration. This is a jurisprudential exclusion affirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of energy (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of energy such as regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, electric currents and explosions are not considered subject-matter within the meaning of invention in section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electromagnetic and acoustic signals are considered forms of energy and do not contain matter; they are not an art (method), a process, a machine, or a composition of matter, and therefore not statutory subject-matter. Claims to electromagnetic/acoustic signals do not constitute statutory subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of solely intellectual or aesthetic significance (non-statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that have a purely intellectual or aesthetic significance are considered not to affect the functioning of the invention and cannot change how the practical form operates to solve the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a claim is directed to subject-matter having solely intellectual or aesthetic significance, the claim is defective under section 2. However, if the practical form solves a practical problem and gives rise to new functionality, patentability is not impacted merely because the purpose is non-statutory (intellectual/aesthetic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter (non-functional descriptive matter excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed matter that has purely intellectual or aesthetic significance, such as a literary work, is excluded from patentability for the reasons outlined regarding features of solely intellectual/aesthetic significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where printed matter provides a new functionality to the substrate on which it is printed (i.e., solves a practical problem related to use of the printed matter), a claim may be statutory. Examples: textile markings enabling precision in manufacturing; newspaper layout facilitating folding/reading; text layout facilitating bookbinding; ticket layout permitting division while retaining information. 'Printed matter' includes any means of displaying information, not just ink-on-paper. Example analysis (scratch-off lottery ticket maze) shows printed matter that provides no new functionality is non-statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine arts (non-statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fine art is that having intellectual meaning or aesthetic appeal alone, and fine arts are not patentable subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes activities such as dancing, acting, writing, painting, playing musical instruments, etc. Products derived from fine art are generally non-statutory. The exclusion does not extend to inventive materials and instruments used in practising a fine art (e.g., an inventive easel, paints, or brushes may be patentable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schemes, plans, rules, and mental processes (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme, plan, or rule for performing an operation, achieving a result or controlling a method, and a process that is exclusively a series of mental steps (e.g., performing calculations; manipulating data to produce a different purely intellectual meaning) are disembodied (abstract) and not a practical form of an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such purely mental or abstract processes are non-statutory regardless of reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Games (methods of playing) (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: A manner of playing a game or sport does not solve a practical problem and a method for playing a game is therefore non-statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies whether the claimed method is based on rules governing play or actions to achieve game-related results. Tools used in playing a game (e.g., specialized table, playing piece, or game board with a mechanical function) may be patentable on their merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Anticipation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be novel; novelty requires that individual disclosures in the prior art do not anticipate the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation is assessed claim-by-claim by asking whether the prior disclosure, when understood by the person skilled in the art in light of their common general knowledge, provides both a description of the claimed invention (disclosure) and sufficient instructions to enable the invention to be practised (enablement). The comparison is based on the essential elements of the claim, properly construed, to the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (section 28.2 summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 28.2 of the Patent Act defines what disclosures may be considered for assessing anticipation: it establishes a grace period for applicant-originating disclosures, treats third-party disclosures worldwide before the claim date as prior art, and sets conditions for first-to-file co-pending applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International (PCT) applications are not Canadian applications for first-to-file anticipation unless they have entered the national phase. A Canadian application withdrawn before being opened to public inspection is considered never filed for first-to-file prior art purposes; opened-to-public-inspection applications may be eligible as prior art even if withdrawn/abandoned/refused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-anticipation and applicant grace period
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 28.2(1)(a): subject-matter defined by a claim must not have been disclosed before the one-year period immediately preceding the filing date (or before the claim date if earlier) by the applicant or by a person who obtained knowledge from the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines self-anticipation and excludes disclosures made within the one-year grace period from being prior art. The grace period is one year before the filing date unless the claim date is earlier, in which case it is the period between the claim date and the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party anticipation (third-party public disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 28.2(1)(b): subject-matter must not have been disclosed before the claim date by a person other than the applicant such that the subject-matter became available to the public in Canada or elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines public disclosures by third parties anywhere in the world prior to the claim date as prior art for assessing anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-file anticipation (earlier Canadian filing date) — paragraph 28.2(1)(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 28.2(1)(c): subject-matter must not have been disclosed in an application for a patent filed in Canada by a person other than the applicant that has a filing date before the claim date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives effect to first-to-file considerations: a Canadian patent application not open to public inspection as of the subject application's claim date may nevertheless be considered for anticipation. The entire content of the earlier application is considered; analysis is not limited to matter claimed in the earlier application. Examiners should obtain priority documents when applicability depends on priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-file anticipation (priority-date based) — paragraph 28.2(1)(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 28.2(1)(d): expands prior art to include a co-pending Canadian application filed by another person with conditions (i)-(iv) relating to previous regular filings, priority dates, 12-month filing window, and a request for priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires that claims of the co-pending application benefit from a priority date that precedes the claim date of the pending application; examiner should review filing date, priority request information, and priority document content. Assessment is based on entirety of information benefiting from the priority date, not limited by the co-pending application's claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing anticipation (Apotex test: disclosure + enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test requires that a single prior disclosure both disclose and enable the claimed invention. The first part asks whether a single prior teaching discloses the same invention (or at least one operating embodiment) when read by a person skilled in the art in a purposive manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior disclosure need not be an exact description; if carrying out the directions in the prior disclosure would inevitably result in infringement of the examined claim, it discloses the same invention. The second part asks whether the prior disclosure enables operation without inventive effort or undue experimentation. For enablement, the skilled person is assumed willing to make trial-and-error experiments that are not inventive or an undue burden. If unclear, examiner must explain reasons for concluding disclosure is enabling. Reverse infringement principle ('what amounts to infringement, if posterior, should amount to anticipation, if anterior') can be used. Analyse essential elements of the claim; non-essential elements need not be disclosed. For claims covering multiple embodiments, anticipation of any one enabled embodiment suffices. Distinguish proper combinations vs aggregations; assess each collocated distinct invention individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by prior sale or use
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale or use of an invention can be relevant prior art if it provides an enabling disclosure of the application's claimed subject-matter prior to the claim date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be considered disclosed, the prior sale/use must provide the skilled person sufficient information to comprehend the invention; the public must have had the opportunity to access the information. Reverse engineering the product by known analytical techniques may be relevant — reverse engineering must be possible without inventive effort. The applicant's grace period (paragraph 28.2(1)(a)) applies to prior making available by the applicant or persons who obtained knowledge from the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit or inherent disclosure in prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An enabling disclosure is considered to disclose everything that would inevitably or necessarily occur or be done by a person practising the invention; inherent and implicit features of a prior disclosure are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherent features include properties/characteristics necessarily present (e.g., material ductility, mechanism of action). Implicit features include what the skilled person would necessarily understand to be part of practising the disclosure (e.g., means to reduce pressure). Mere discovery of properties of a previously disclosed invention does not render it newly patentable; however, discovery that leads to a new practical application may be patentable. If anticipation requires an inherent/implicit feature, examiner must clearly explain the basis for concluding the feature is implicit or inherent.
